name: Jandoquile v. Revilla, Jr.
subject: Legal and Judicial Ethics
facts: Atty. Quirino P. Revilla, Jr., a notary public, notarized a complaint-affidavit signed by three people: Heneraline L. Brosas (the sister of his wife), Herizalyn Brosas Pedrosa (his wife's sister-in-law), and Elmer L. Alvarado (the live-in houseboy of the Brosas family). He did not ask any of them to show valid ID cards. Bernard N. Jandoquile filed a complaint asking the Supreme Court to disbar him. Atty. Revilla, Jr. admitted the facts. He argued that this single act is not a ground for disbarment, that he acted more as the three signers' lawyer than as a notary public, and that he did not need their IDs because he knows them personally.
issue: Should Atty. Revilla, Jr. be disbarred for (1) notarizing a complaint-affidavit signed by relatives of his wife, and (2) not asking the signers to show valid ID cards?
ruling: No disbarment, but he was penalized. (1) He violated the disqualification rule in Section 3(c), Rule IV of the 2004 Rules on Notarial Practice, because two of the signers are his relatives within the fourth civil degree of affinity (relatives through marriage). He should have refused to notarize. The Court rejected his claim that he acted as their lawyer and not as a notary public: the notarial certificate at the bottom of the document bore his signature as a notary public. (2) He was not liable for skipping the IDs. A notary public who knows the signers personally need not ask for their IDs, as shown by the definition of a jurat. But he was at fault for not stating in the jurat that he knows them personally. (3) His violation was not deceit, malpractice, gross misconduct, gross immoral conduct, or any other serious ground for disbarment under Section 27, Rule 138 of the Rules of Court. Since disbarment should not be imposed when a lighter penalty will do, he was reprimanded and disqualified from being commissioned as a notary public, or from performing any notarial act, for three months. He was also told to inform the Court by affidavit once those three months are over.
keyDoctrine: A notary public may not notarize a document if the principal (the person whose act is being notarized) is a relative by affinity or consanguinity within the fourth civil degree, even if the notary is also that person's lawyer. A notary who personally knows the signers need not ask for their IDs, but should say in the jurat that they are personally known. A single violation like this is not a ground for disbarment; a lighter penalty is enough.

name: Zulueta v. Court of Appeals
subject: Communication Law
facts: Cecilia Zulueta is the wife of Dr. Alfredo Martin. On March 26, 1982, she entered her husband's medical clinic and, in the presence of her mother, a driver, and his secretary, forcibly opened the drawers and cabinet there. She took 157 documents and papers: private letters between Dr. Martin and his alleged mistresses, greeting cards, cancelled checks, diaries, his passport, and photographs. She wanted to use them as evidence in the case she had filed against him for legal separation and for disqualification from practicing medicine. Dr. Martin sued to get the papers back and for damages. The trial court ruled for him, ordered her to return the papers, made her pay damages, and barred her and her lawyers from using the papers as evidence. The Court of Appeals agreed. Zulueta's only argument before the Supreme Court was that in an earlier disbarment case against her lawyer (Martin v. Felix, Jr.), the Court had already ruled these papers admissible as evidence.
issue: Are the papers that the wife took from her husband's clinic, without his knowledge and consent, admissible as evidence, on the theory that the Court already held them admissible in the earlier disbarment case against her lawyer?
ruling: No. The petition was denied. (1) The earlier case did not decide that the papers were admissible. The lawyer was cleared in that case only because, when he used the papers, the trial court's order banning their use was temporarily stopped by the Supreme Court's restraining order (TRO). Once that TRO was lifted, the ban applied again. (2) The papers are inadmissible. The Constitution says the privacy of communication and correspondence is inviolable, and this applies even when the person who violated it is the wife. The only exceptions are a lawful order of the court, or when public safety or order requires otherwise, as prescribed by law. Evidence obtained in violation of this is inadmissible for any purpose in any proceeding. (3) Marriage does not take away a person's right to privacy. The intimacies between husband and wife do not justify either one breaking into the other's drawers and cabinets to look for evidence of infidelity. The law protects free communication between spouses by making it privileged, but freedom of communication is different from forcing each spouse to share everything they know with the other.
keyDoctrine: The constitutional right to privacy of communication and correspondence (1987 Constitution, Art. III, Sec. 3) applies even between husband and wife. Evidence obtained in violation of it is inadmissible for any purpose in any proceeding. The only exceptions are a lawful order of the court, or when public safety or order requires otherwise, as prescribed by law. A person does not give up their right to privacy by getting married.
